[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Asynchronous Actions and Polling in Ansible"},{"order":2,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"By default, Ansible tasks run synchronously. When you execute a task, Ansible waits for the command to finish on the remote host before moving to the next task or host. However, some tasks like large software updates, system reboots, or complex database migrations take a long time. For these scenarios, Ansible provides asynchronous mode and polling."},{"order":4,"type":"subheading","text":"Key Concepts: async and poll"},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"async: Defines the maximum time in seconds that a task is allowed to run. If the task exceeds this limit, Ansible kills the process on the remote node."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"poll: Defines how often (in seconds) Ansible should check back on the task status. If poll is set to 0, Ansible fires the task and immediately moves to the next task without waiting for results (fire-and-forget)."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Example 1: Running a Long Task with Polling"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"The following playbook runs a script that takes up to 600 seconds to complete. Ansible checks the status every 30 seconds."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"---
- name: Run a long running task asynchronously
  hosts: all
  tasks:
    - name: Execute heavy script
      ansible.builtin.shell: /usr/local/bin/heavy_script.sh
      async: 600
      poll: 30"},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Example 2: Fire-and-Forget (poll: 0)"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"Sometimes you need to trigger an action, like a system reboot or starting a background daemon, without waiting for the task to finish. Setting poll to 0 achieves this behavior."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"---
- name: Fire and forget example
  hosts: all
  tasks:
    - name: Restart remote server
      ansible.builtin.reboot:
      async: 300
      poll: 0
    
    - name: Continue with other tasks immediately
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "The server is rebooting in the background.""},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Checking Results Later with async_status"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"When you use poll: 0, Ansible returns a job ID. You can capture this job ID using the register keyword and check its status later in the playbook using the ansible.builtin.async_status module."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"---
- name: Check async job status
  hosts: all
  tasks:
    - name: Start long operation
      ansible.builtin.command: /usr/bin/long_process
      async: 3600
      poll: 0
      register: jellyfish

    - name: Do other work here...
      ansible.builtin.pause:
        seconds: 5

    - name: Check the status of the async task
      ansible.builtin.async_status:
        jid: "{{ jellyfish.ansible_job_id }}"
      register: job_result
      until: job_result.finished
      retries: 30
      delay: 10"},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"Asynchronous actions and polling are essential tools in Ansible for managing long-running operations efficiently. By properly configuring async and poll limits, or utilizing fire-and-forget strategies with async_status, you can optimize your automation workflows for performance and scalability."}]
